planting.note: Pot divisions or keikis in a coarse bark-and-sphagnum mix in a slatted or clear container; Phalaenopsis sanderiana is a warm-growing Mindanao species best kept out of direct sun at an east window or a few feet back from a bright south or west exposure.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light in a coarse bark or bark-and-sphagnum mix, letting the medium approach dryness between thorough waterings rather than keeping it constantly wet. Phalaenopsis sanderiana is a warm-growing Philippine species restricted to Mindanao, closely related to P. schilleriana but with plain dark green leaves instead of silver mottling and blush-pink flowers set off by a boldly striped, contrasting lip. Its long, gently arching sprays typically open in late summer and fall and can carry a few dozen flowers on a well-grown plant, and cutting a spent spike back to a lower node sometimes coaxes a second flush of bloom.

common_name: Christmas Orchid (Maxima Cattleya, Flor de Noviembre)

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in a basket with coarse bark and generous airflow around the roots; Cattleya maxima flowers in late fall to early winter and should not be disturbed while a bloom sheath is developing at the top of the newest pseudobulb.

directions: Mount on a slab or grow in a basket with coarse bark and generous airflow around the roots, providing bright indirect to lightly filtered direct sun for best flowering. Cattleya maxima is a unifoliate species native to the Pacific slopes of Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia, where growers call it the Christmas orchid for its habit of opening large, ruffled lavender-pink flowers with a boldly veined magenta-and-white trumpet lip around the November-December holidays. Water freely while new growths and roots are actively developing, then ease off markedly once growth matures so the plant experiences the pronounced dry season this Andean species knows in habitat. Because flower spikes emerge from a sheath at the top of the newest pseudobulb, avoid damaging the sheath tip when repotting or moving the plant.

planting.note: Repot after flowering into a shallow basket or clay pot with coarse, fast-draining bark; Cattleya gaskelliana tolerates somewhat lower light and cooler nights than many large-flowered Cattleyas, making it a forgiving choice for a bright windowsill.

directions: Grow mounted or in a shallow basket with coarse, fast-draining bark, giving bright indirect to lightly filtered direct sun and generous humidity. Cattleya gaskelliana is a unifoliate species from the coastal ranges of Venezuela and Colombia that opens large, softly fragrant flowers in shades of pale lavender to near-white, with a deep magenta-purple, gold-throated lip, typically in early to midsummer. It tolerates slightly lower light and cooler nights than many large-flowered Cattleyas, making it one of the more forgiving unifoliate species for a home windowsill or lightly shaded greenhouse bench. Water thoroughly as new growths develop, then allow the mix to dry noticeably between waterings once the newest pseudobulb has matured.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or grow in a basket that lets the long canes arch and hang; Dendrobium aphyllum needs a pronounced cool, dry winter rest with only occasional misting once the thin canes shed their leaves ahead of spring bloom.

directions: Mount on a slab or grow in a basket that allows the long, slender canes to arch and eventually hang, since Dendrobium aphyllum is naturally a pendulous, cane-forming epiphyte of the Himalayan foothills, northeastern India, and mainland Southeast Asia. Give it a pronounced cool, dry rest in winter with only occasional misting once the thin canes shed their leaves, then resume regular watering in early spring as flower buds swell along the bare nodes. The pale lilac-pink, papery flowers open in profusion along the length of last year's leafless canes before new growth emerges, filling the air with a light, sweet fragrance for several weeks. Provide bright filtered light and good airflow year-round, and avoid disturbing the roots except when the basket or mount has clearly broken down.

planting.note: Grow in a basket or clay pot with coarse bark positioned so the dense, pendulous flower trusses can hang freely below the pseudobulbs; give a distinct cooler, drier rest once the season's growth matures and leaves begin to fall.

directions: Grow in a basket or clay pot with coarse bark, positioning the plant where the dense, pendulous flower trusses can hang freely below the pseudobulbs. Dendrobium densiflorum is a Himalayan and Southeast Asian species that produces tightly packed, rounded racemes of golden-yellow flowers with a vivid orange, fringed lip in spring, closely resembling its relatives D. chrysotoxum and D. thyrsiflorum but with an even more compact, ball-like inflorescence. Water and fertilize generously while the current season's pseudobulbs are actively elongating, then impose a distinct cooler, drier rest once growth matures and leaves begin to fall, resuming water only as new flower spikes appear. Bright light with some protection from the harshest midday sun keeps the stout, four-angled pseudobulbs compact and encourages the heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Grow in a basket or clay pot with coarse bark in bright indirect to lightly filtered direct light; leave spent-looking flower spikes on Oncidium leucochilum in place, since the same spike often reblooms from side branches over several months.

directions: Grow in a basket or clay pot with coarse bark, providing bright indirect to lightly filtered direct light and a distinct drier rest once the current season's growth matures. Oncidium leucochilum is a robust, clump-forming species from the seasonally dry oak-pine forests of Mexico and Central America that sends up tall, branching sprays bearing dozens of yellow-green flowers heavily barred in chestnut brown, each with a crisp white, butterfly-shaped lip that gives the species its name. The flower spikes can persist and rebloom from side branches over several months, so leave a spent-looking spike in place rather than cutting it back immediately. Water generously while roots and new growths are active, then reduce sharply in winter to mimic the pronounced dry season this species experiences in the wild.

planting.note: Repot back-bulb divisions in early spring into a coarse, bark-based cymbidium mix; Cymbidium erythrostylum benefits from cooler nights in autumn to help initiate its upright, outward-facing flower spikes.

directions: Repot back-bulb divisions in early spring into a coarse, bark-based cymbidium mix, and grow in bright filtered light with cooler nights in autumn to help initiate flower spikes. Cymbidium erythrostylum is a compact species from the Annam highlands of central Vietnam, notable among Cymbidium species for its upright, outward-facing flowers rather than the pendulous or arching sprays typical of the genus, with crisp white sepals and petals set off by a red-streaked lip and the vivid crimson column that gives the species its name. It has been used extensively by breeders to introduce white coloring and a more compact, upright habit into modern standard cymbidium hybrids. Water freely through the growing season and allow the mix to dry somewhat between waterings once pseudobulbs mature, repotting only every two to three years since the plant flowers best when moderately pot-bound.
